crux.for_the_english: Keep two audible Englishes unblended: Nekohachi in a working, comic, self-interrupting stage patter full of swallowed retorts and asides, the writers in flat, borrowed critical abstraction; never polish either into the same literary fluency, and let the reader feel when neither fully understands the other.
crux.point: The collision of languages is the action: close third-person narration saturated with Nekohachi's Edokko yose patter (でげす, な, self-deprecating jokes, internal 洒落 he performs even to himself) set against the literati's imported jargon (シチュエイション, バック, 現実主義/具体) that he literally cannot parse. He is never off stage—he swallows '小奈良の小大仏' (p8), turns a tram ride into a 高座 (p5-9), negotiates every humiliation as a gag—while they study that very compulsion as '悲哀' in Kume's '虎'.
crux.why: Strip the register gap and the plot (a mimic taken to a research society) has no tension left: his mishearings of 'situation' as a predicament he is trapped in (p53), his gratitude at being quoted back as criticism (p79-82), and his final triumph in performance (p124-136) all only register because we hear him thinking and speaking in a different tongue from theirs.

crux.for_the_english: Hold the double exposure in the English: render his self-recognitions and the closing humility straight, without irony markers, ennoblement, or a softened/resolved ending, so the reader—not the prose—decides how much is insight and how much is act.
crux.point: The mirrored tiger must stay unresolved: Nekohachi condemns Fukai for letting his child see the debasing role (p91-95) and has moved to the suburbs to hide his own, yet eagerly performs, fishes for praise and a fee (p171-177), and misreads Kume's anonymous self-denunciation as proof Kume is a wit after his own heart (p103-110). The text itself flags that even his grief-stricken face is partly exaggeration he half-knows about (p91), and ends not in renunciation—he plans to retell the novel to his wife (p188)—but in a 'rare' humble, human feeling (p185) alongside gas-lamp advertising and the night's two coins.
crux.why: If the translation settles him as either dignified artist-victim (the literati's '悲哀' made true) or comic butt the reader pities from above, it picks the side the story refuses: his sorrow is real and performed at once, his pride in hiding the act from his sons coexists with delight that '例の猫八' is known (p37-39), and that undecidability is what the whole mirrored structure was built to produce.

data.say: Confident on both, from the density of register-marked speech and the sustained tiger mirroring; a different contemporary reception history showing the literati's terms were ordinary unmarked speech in 1918 would soften the first, but not remove it.
data.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that Nekohachi's でげす/べらんめい forms were neutral Taishō colloquial rather than class-and-stage marked would weaken crux 1; evidence from the serial context that Iwano framed the ending as straightforward conversion would weaken crux 2.
